articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady I built this with an AI coding agent. The section called My Agent Session says what the agent did. What I Built In August, three psychologists at Binghamton University published a paper in Memory & Cognition called "Digital amnesia: The aftermath of a screenshot." Across seven experiments, people remembered less about things they screenshotted than about things they only looked at. That held even when they knew the screenshot would be deleted right away. So the screenshot is doing the remembering, and the only thing it remembers about itself is the time. My Desktop is full of files like Screenshot 2026-10-09 at 10.12.33 PM.png . One of them is the error I need for a bug report.

articles.title: LayerEditor Revolution: One Prompt, 3 Layers, 1 Second—Designers Are Going Crazy
articles.excerpt: LayerEditor Unleashed: How Compositional Edit‑Prior Distillation Turns One‑Shot Text Edits into Reusable Image Layers The Lead “I typed ‘swap the red car for a blue truck’ and the model gave me three…
articles.body: LayerEditor Unleashed: How Compositional Edit‑Prior Distillation Turns One‑Shot Text Edits into Reusable Image Layers The Lead “ I typed ‘swap the red car for a blue truck’ and the model gave me three separate RGBA stacks in 0.9 seconds ,” reported a designer during the CVPR‑2026 workshop demo. The claim shocked the audience because every diffusion‑based editor up to that point produced a single blended output that users had to mask manually. The new paper Editing Images into Reusable Layers via Compositional Edit‑Prior Distillation (arXiv 2610.24738, Oct 17 2026) flips that assumption on its head. Instead of treating “editing” and “layer extraction” as two unrelated steps, the authors fuse them inside a single diffusion pipeline. They call the resulting system LayerEditor .

articles.title: The DMARC Record a Small Business Should Publish First (and When to Tighten It)
articles.excerpt: If your business sends mail from its own domain (you@yourbusiness.com), three DNS records do the authentication work: SPF, DKIM and DMARC. SPF and DKIM prove a message came from a server you actually…
articles.body: If your business sends mail from its own domain ( you@yourbusiness.com ), three DNS records do the authentication work: SPF, DKIM and DMARC. SPF and DKIM prove a message came from a server you actually use. DMARC tells the receiving server what to do when a message claims to be from your domain but fails those checks, and where to send reports about it. With no DMARC record, anyone can put your domain in the From: line of a phishing email. The receiving server has no instructions from you, and you never hear about it. Start with one TXT record At your DNS host (Cloudflare, GoDaddy, Squarespace, Network Solutions, or wherever your DNS lives), add: Host/Name: _dmarc Type: TXT Value: v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@yourbusiness.com Swap in a mailbox you really own.

articles.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF): When Your Browser Becomes the Attacker
articles.excerpt: Imagine logging into your banking application, then opening another website in a different tab. Without your knowledge, that website triggers a request to your banking application to perform an action…
articles.body: Imagine logging into your banking application, then opening another website in a different tab. Without your knowledge, that website triggers a request to your banking application to perform an action you never authorized. You didn't initiate the action, but your browser may still send your authentication cookies with the request. That's the idea behind Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) . What Is CSRF? Cross-Site Request Forgery is a web security vulnerability that tricks a user's browser into performing unwanted actions on a website where the user is already authenticated. The attacker doesn't necessarily need to steal your password or session cookie. Instead, they exploit the trust between your browser and the application.

articles.title: Refresh tokens in a .NET 10 Minimal API: rotation, reuse detection and revocation
articles.excerpt: In the previous posts of this series I've been building a free .NET 10 Minimal API starter: JWT authentication, per-user ownership, rate limiting and health checks. Until now, login returned a single…
articles.body: In the previous posts of this series I've been building a free .NET 10 Minimal API starter: JWT authentication, per-user ownership, rate limiting and health checks. Until now, login returned a single JWT that lasted 60 minutes. That has two problems: It can't be revoked. If a token leaks, whoever has it keeps access for up to an hour, and "log out" only means the client forgets the token. Shortening it hurts users. A 15-minute token without a way to renew it means logging in again every 15 minutes. Refresh tokens solve both. In this post I'll go through the design I chose, the code, how I tested expiry without waiting a week, and a couple of mistakes I made on the way. The code is in the repo: Fmaes2/dotnet-minimal-api-starter .

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film.

articles.body: It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie.

articles.title: SpaceX launches Starlink satellites from California as Falcon 9 cadence slows (video)
articles.excerpt: SpaceX sent 27 more of its Starlink broadband satellites to orbit today (Oct. 23), in its first Starlink launch in 11 days.
articles.body: SpaceX launched its newest batch of Starlink broadband internet satellites today (Oct. 23) from the California coast. The spacecraft, Starlink Group 15-15, were stacked 27 high inside the payload fairing of a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket , which lifted off from Pad 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base at 6:48 p.m. EDT (2248 GMT; 3:48 p.m. local time in California). The rocket's first stage booster, designated B1063, executed its main engine cutoff and stage separation about 2.5 minutes into flight, sending the second stage to continue onward to low Earth orbit (LEO). The vehicle's two-piece protective payload fairing was jettisoned just before T+3 minutes. A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launches 27 Starlink satellites from California on Oct. 23, 2026.
